body.heading: Light from falling electrons
paragraphs: Inside an LED, electricity pushes electrons through a semiconductor crystal engineered with an energy step. When an electron drops across that step, it gives up its extra energy as a single particle of light — a photon. No filament, no flame, nothing has to glow hot.

The size of the step sets the colour: bigger steps produce blue light, smaller steps red. White bulbs usually start with a blue LED and add a phosphor coating that converts part of the blue into yellows and reds, mixing to white.

body.heading: Why so little waste heat
paragraphs: An old filament bulb makes light by heating a wire until it glows, and about 90 percent of its energy escapes as heat rather than light. An LED skips the heating entirely, so it needs far less electricity for the same brightness — typically about 75 percent less.

LEDs still warm up a little, and their electronics dislike heat, which is why LED bulbs have metal fins or heavy bases: those are heat sinks, drawing warmth away from the chip to keep it efficient and long-lived. Keep an LED cool and it can outlast the fitting it is screwed into.

body.heading: Built to last
paragraphs: With no filament to burn out or glass envelope to shatter, an LED bulb is rated for around 25,000 hours of use — roughly twenty years of evenings. Most failures, when they come, are in the small power-supply electronics, not the light-emitting chip itself.

The savings compound quietly: swap ten filament bulbs for LEDs and a household can cut its lighting electricity by three-quarters, while changing bulbs becomes a rare event rather than a monthly chore.
